sectionTitle: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)
topic: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Even though no atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, it is not always possible to obtain the calculated amount of a product because:
the reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible
some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture
some of the reactants may react in ways different to the expected reaction.
The amount of a product obtained is known as the yield. When compared with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage, it is called the percentage yield.
% Yield= (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) ×100
calculate the percentage yield of a product from the actual yield of a reaction
(HT only) calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction.

The atom economy (atom utilisation) is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons to use reactions with high atom economy.
The percentage atom economy of a reaction is calculated using the balanced equation for the reaction as follows:
(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) ×100
calculate the atom economy of a reaction to form a desired product from the balanced equation

(HT only) explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification places the derivation of a theoretical mass at Higher tier only. Every percentage yield item written for both tiers therefore prints the maximum theoretical mass in the stem, so a Foundation student never has to derive it. Only q09 and q10, both tiered 'higher', ask for a theoretical mass to be worked out from a mass of reactant and the balanced equation, and both print the equation and the relative formula masses required.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Pathway choice is Higher tier only, and the specification supplies the data rather than asking students to recall it. q16 is tiered 'higher' and gives atom economy, percentage yield, rate and the fate of the by-product for two routes; the student weighs the figures given and is never asked to recall industrial process detail or to calculate an equilibrium position.

concepts.definition: The mass of product that would form if every reactant particle reacted exactly as the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly be made, so it is the figure the mass actually obtained is compared with.

concepts.term: Conservation of mass in a reaction
concepts.definition: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction. A shortfall on the balance therefore never means that atoms have disappeared; it means atoms are somewhere other than in the product that was collected and weighed.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. Such a reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is always still present and the amount of product obtained is below the theoretical maximum.

Product left behind when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals clinging to the filter paper or the beaker, or solid still dissolved in the liquid poured away. It was made but never weighed, so the yield falls.

A reaction in which some of the reactants react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming a substance other than the desired product. The atoms are all still present but they are locked into the wrong compound.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is a measured quantity, found by weighing the product after it has been separated from the mixture, washed and dried.
The amount of product obtained compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage: % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.

concepts.term: Finding a theoretical mass from the balanced equation
concepts.definition: Convert the given mass of reactant to moles, use the balancing numbers in the equation to find the moles of the desired product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of that product. The balancing numbers must be used or the answer is out by that factor.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation alone, using relative formula masses, so it is fixed for a given reaction whatever happens in the laboratory.

concepts.term: Why a high atom economy matters
concepts.definition: A reaction with a high atom economy turns more of the starting materials into the product that is wanted. This is important for sustainable development, because raw materials are limited and waste has to be dealt with, and for economic reasons, because unused starting material and waste disposal both cost money.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Every reactant in the equation counts in the bottom line, each multiplied by its balancing number.

misconceptions.question: No atoms are gained or lost in a reaction, so why is less product collected than the calculation predicts?
misconceptions.correct: Every atom still exists. They are simply not all in the product collected: the reaction may not have gone to completion because it is reversible, some product may have been lost when it was separated from the reaction mixture, or some reactants may have reacted in ways different to the expected reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: If there is less product than the calculation predicts, some atoms must have been used up or destroyed along the way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is learnt as a rule about sealed flasks, so when the balance reads short students look for missing matter instead of asking where the matter went.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the atoms are, not whether they still exist. Name one of the three destinations the specification allows: still unreacted, left behind during separation, or built into a different product.

misconceptions.question: Does a yield below 100 % show that mass was not conserved?
misconceptions.correct: No. Mass is conserved in every chemical reaction, sealed or open. A low yield describes where the product ended up, not how much matter exists.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is only conserved if the reaction is carried out in a sealed container, so an open reaction can genuinely lose mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet conservation of mass through demonstrations in stoppered flasks and meet apparent mass changes in open crucibles, so they attach the law to the apparatus rather than to the atoms.
misconceptions.correction: In an open vessel the atoms leave the vessel; they are not destroyed. Weighing everything, including any gas, always gives the same total.

misconceptions.question: Why does a reversible reaction limit the yield?
misconceptions.correct: The reaction does not go to completion. Product re-forms reactant as fast as reactant forms product, so some reactant is always left and the yield is below the maximum.
misconceptions.misconception: In a reversible reaction all the product eventually turns back into reactants, so no product can be collected at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The double arrow is read as 'it goes backwards' rather than as 'both directions happen at the same time', so students imagine the forward reaction being completely undone.
misconceptions.correction: Both reactions run together and settle at a balance point. There is always some product present, just less than the equation on its own predicts.

misconceptions.question: Crystals are filtered, washed and dried before weighing. Why is the mass below the theoretical maximum?
misconceptions.correct: Some of the product is lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture: crystals stay on the filter paper and on the glassware, and some solid remains dissolved in the liquid poured away.
misconceptions.misconception: Filtering and washing take atoms out of the compound itself, so what is left weighs less than it should.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'lost' is read as a loss from each particle rather than as a loss of whole particles from the sample being weighed.
misconceptions.correction: Separation removes some of the crystals, not part of each crystal. What is weighed is pure product; there is simply less of it.

misconceptions.question: An unexpected second compound is found in the product mixture. Which reason for a low yield does this show?
misconceptions.correct: Some of the reactants reacted in ways different to the expected reaction, so those atoms are locked into a substance that is not the desired product.
misconceptions.misconception: Any unexpected substance in the mixture must mean that the reaction was reversible.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reversibility is the first reason students learn and becomes a catch-all explanation for anything that is not the pure expected product.
misconceptions.correction: A reversible reaction leaves the original reactants behind, not a brand new compound. A new compound points to some reactant taking a different reaction pathway.

misconceptions.question: What does percentage yield compare?
misconceptions.correct: The mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass of that product, as a percentage.
misconceptions.misconception: Percentage yield compares the mass of product with the mass of reactants that were used, or reports the percentage that was lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It sounds like an efficiency, and the reactant mass is the first number the student weighed out, so it feels like the natural thing to divide by.
misconceptions.correction: The comparison is product against predicted product, and it is the amount obtained that goes on top, not the amount missing.

misconceptions.question: Which way round does the percentage yield fraction go?
misconceptions.correct: % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100, so the answer can never be above 100 %.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the maximum theoretical mass by the mass actually made.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that two masses are divided but not which one is on top, and the theoretical mass is the larger number, which feels like a natural numerator.
misconceptions.correction: Check the answer: a yield above 100 % is impossible, so any answer over 100 % means the fraction was written upside down.

misconceptions.question: A student divides 54 by 60 and writes 0.9. What has been missed?
misconceptions.correct: The ratio must be multiplied by 100 to turn it into a percentage, giving 90.0 %.
misconceptions.misconception: The decimal answer from the division is the percentage yield.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The division feels like the chemistry, so the x 100 at the end of the formula is treated as decoration and dropped.
misconceptions.correction: A percentage is a number per hundred. If the answer comes out as a decimal below 1, the x 100 has been forgotten.

misconceptions.question: A stem gives a reactant mass, a theoretical mass and an actual mass. Which two are used?
misconceptions.correct: The mass of product actually made and the maximum theoretical mass of product. The reactant mass is not used in the percentage yield calculation at all.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the mass of product made by the mass of reactant that was weighed out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactant mass is usually the first number in the question, and students who have not fixed the formula reach for the number they met first.
misconceptions.correction: Both masses in the fraction refer to the same product. If one of the numbers is a reactant, it does not belong in the fraction.

misconceptions.question: What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide from 10 g of calcium carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: 10 g of CaCO3 is 0.1 mol, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the theoretical mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is conserved, so 10 g of calcium carbonate must give 10 g of calcium oxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is over-applied: the total mass of all the products is 10 g, but the carbon dioxide escapes and carries part of it away.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is conserved across all the products together, not for one product on its own. Work in moles and use the relative formula mass of the product asked for.

misconceptions.question: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Why is 7 g of iron from 20 g of iron(III) oxide wrong?
misconceptions.correct: 0.125 mol of Fe2O3 gives 0.25 mol of Fe because of the 2 in front of Fe, so the mass is 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.
misconceptions.misconception: One mole of iron(III) oxide gives one mole of iron, so the balancing numbers can be ignored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students convert mass to moles confidently and then jump straight to the relative formula mass of the product, skipping the mole ratio step entirely.
misconceptions.correction: Always read the balancing numbers as a mole ratio. Write the ratio down, here 1 : 2, before multiplying by the relative formula mass.

misconceptions.question: Can the relative formula masses in the equation be used directly as masses in grams?
misconceptions.correct: No. A relative formula mass gives the mass of one mole, so it must be scaled by the number of moles actually present.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers taken from the equation, such as 2 x 56 = 112, are the answer in grams, or they can be divided either way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The relative formula masses are the most visible numbers in the working, so students report them, or combine them as a ratio without checking which way up it goes.
misconceptions.correction: Ask how many moles there are. Only when it is exactly one mole does the relative formula mass equal the mass in grams.

misconceptions.question: What does atom economy measure?
misconceptions.correct: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as the useful product, worked out from the balanced equation.
misconceptions.misconception: Atom economy tells you how much of the predicted product you actually managed to collect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Yield and atom economy are taught together, both are percentages and both describe efficiency, so the two definitions blur into one.
misconceptions.correction: Yield is measured in the laboratory and changes with technique; atom economy comes from the equation and is the same every time the reaction is used.

misconceptions.question: Which masses are used to calculate the percentage atom economy?
misconceptions.correct: Relative formula masses taken from the balanced equation. Masses measured in the laboratory are never used.
misconceptions.misconception: Weigh the reactants and the product, then divide one measured mass by the other, correcting for anything lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentage yield uses masses from the balance, so students assume the other percentage in this topic must use them too.
misconceptions.correction: Atom economy is fixed by the equation. It is the same figure whether the reaction is done well or badly, and on any scale.

misconceptions.question: What goes on the bottom of the atom economy fraction, and what goes on top?
misconceptions.correct: The sum of the relative formula masses of all the reactants from the equation goes underneath, and the relative formula mass of the desired product, including its balancing number, goes on top.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the reactant that contains the desired product needs to be counted, and balancing numbers can be left out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trace the atoms of interest back to one reactant and treat the other reactants as if they were not really starting materials.
misconceptions.correction: Every reactant had to be supplied and paid for, so every reactant counts in the bottom line, each multiplied by its balancing number.

misconceptions.question: Why is an atom economy of 566.7 % impossible?
misconceptions.correct: The desired product cannot have more mass than all the reactants together, so the answer must be 100 % or less.
misconceptions.misconception: The fraction can be written either way up, so a value above 100 % is acceptable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula is remembered as two relative formula masses divided, with no check on which one is the numerator.
misconceptions.correction: Put the desired product on top. Any answer above 100 % shows that the fraction was inverted.

misconceptions.question: Is the atom economy always 100 % because no atoms are lost?
misconceptions.correct: No. All the atoms are still present, but those in the by-products are not in the useful product, so the atom economy is below 100 % whenever the equation shows more than one product.
misconceptions.misconception: Since no atoms are gained or lost, all of the starting material ends up as useful product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is confused with usefulness: students count all the atoms as 'used' whichever compound they end up in.
misconceptions.correction: Only one product is wanted. The atom economy is 100 % only when the equation shows a single product.

misconceptions.question: Route 1 has the higher percentage yield and the faster rate. Does that make it the better pathway?
misconceptions.correct: Not on its own. A high yield from a reaction that wastes most of its atoms still turns a large part of the raw material into waste, so atom economy and the usefulness of the by-products must be weighed as well.
misconceptions.misconception: The route with the higher percentage yield, or the faster rate, is always the better route.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Yield and rate are the more familiar figures and the larger number looks better, so one figure is treated as the whole answer.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the figures separately: yield says how much of the possible product was captured, atom economy says how much of the raw material could ever have become product.

misconceptions.question: Does a high atom economy guarantee a high percentage yield?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are independent. A reaction with a single product has an atom economy of 100 % but may still be reversible or lose product on separation, giving a low yield.
misconceptions.misconception: A high atom economy means most of the product will be collected, so the yield must be high as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are percentages describing efficiency, so students expect them to rise and fall together.
misconceptions.correction: Atom economy comes from the equation, yield from the laboratory. Either one can be high while the other is low.

mcqs.stem: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the mass of product collected is almost always less than the calculated amount. What does this shortfall show?

options.text: A few of the atoms are destroyed as the old bonds are broken apart.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a shortfall on the balance as matter disappearing rather than as matter sitting somewhere else.

options.text: Mass is conserved only when a reaction is done in a sealed flask.
options.rationale: Picked by students who tie the law to the apparatus, so an open reaction seems to be allowed to lose matter outright.

options.text: The atoms all still exist, but they are not all in the product.
options.rationale: Correct: no atoms are gained or lost, so the missing mass is unreacted material, product lost on separation, or atoms built into a different product.

options.text: The balanced equation overstates how much product could form.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who trust the practical completely and look for the fault in the equation instead of in the apparatus.

mcqs.stem: A product is made using a reaction that is reversible. Why does this keep the yield below the maximum theoretical amount?

options.text: The reaction does not go to completion, so some reactant is left over.
options.rationale: Correct: product re-forms reactant as fast as reactant forms product, so the mixture always still contains some reactant.

options.text: All of the product turns back into the reactants, and none is left.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the double arrow as the forward reaction being completely undone.

options.text: Atoms are used up by the backward reaction and cannot be got back.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think the reverse reaction consumes matter rather than rebuilding the reactants.

options.text: The backward reaction uses up the catalyst, so the reaction ends.
options.rationale: Attractive to students who explain every incomplete reaction by blaming the catalyst, which is not used up.

mcqs.stem: Copper sulfate crystals are filtered from the reaction mixture, washed and dried before being weighed. Which reason for a low yield does this practical show?

options.text: Filtering strips atoms out of the compound, so it now weighs less.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'product lost' as a loss from each particle rather than as a loss of whole particles.

options.text: Water driven off during drying shows mass is not conserved.
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat any fall in mass in an open dish as a breach of conservation of mass.

options.text: Washing adds impurities to the crystals and lowers the mass.
options.rationale: Attractive because washing sounds as if it changes the solid, but added impurities would raise a mass, not lower it.

options.text: Some product stays on the filter paper and inside the glassware.
options.rationale: Correct: product lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture is never weighed, so the yield falls below the maximum.

mcqs.stem: A student analyses the product mixture and finds an unexpected second compound in it. Which reason for the reduced yield does this point to?

options.text: The reaction is reversible, so some product has changed back again.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who use reversibility as a catch-all, but that would leave the original reactants, not a new compound.

options.text: Some reactant reacted in a way different to the expected one.
options.rationale: Correct: a compound that does not appear in the equation shows that some of the reactants took a different reaction pathway.

options.text: Some of the product was spilled while the mixture was poured out.
options.rationale: A real cause of a low yield, but spilling removes product; it cannot create a compound that was not there before.

options.text: The relative formula masses used in the calculation were wrong.
options.rationale: Picked by students who assume the practical was faultless and look for the error in the arithmetic instead.

mcqs.stem: What does the percentage yield of a reaction tell you?

options.text: The percentage of the reactants that have reacted after a fixed time.
options.rationale: Confuses yield with how far a reaction has got, which is a question about rate and completion rather than about mass of product.

options.text: The mass of product made, as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass.
options.rationale: Correct: the amount of product obtained is the yield, and comparing it with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage gives the percentage yield.

options.text: The mass of product made, as a percentage of the mass of the reactants.
options.rationale: A very common substitution: the reactant mass is the number weighed out first, so it feels like the right thing to divide by.

options.text: The percentage of reactant atoms ending up in the useful product.
options.rationale: This is the definition of atom economy, not of yield, and is the classic swap between the two percentages in this topic.

mcqs.stem: Which calculation gives the percentage yield of a product?

options.text: (maximum theoretical mass of product / mass of the product made) x 100
options.rationale: The fraction inverted. Students recall that two masses are divided but put the larger one on top, which allows impossible answers above 100 %.

options.text: (mass of product actually made / total mass of all reactants) x 100
options.rationale: Uses a reactant mass in the bottom line, which belongs to no formula in this topic.

options.text: (Mr of the desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100
options.rationale: This is the atom economy formula, chosen by students who have merged the two percentages together.

options.text: (mass of product actually made / maximum theoretical mass) x 100
options.rationale: Correct: the specification formula is % Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100.

mcqs.stem: 6.0 g of magnesium is burned in air. The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 10.0 g. The student collects 8.5 g of magnesium oxide. What is the percentage yield?

options.rationale: 8.5 / 6.0 x 100, using the mass of magnesium as the denominator instead of the theoretical mass of the product.
8.5 / 10.0 with the x 100 left out, then labelled as a percentage anyway.
10.0 / 8.5 x 100. The fraction is inverted, giving the impossible result of a yield above 100 %.

mcqs.stem: The maximum theoretical mass of a product is 60 g. A student separates and dries the product and obtains 54 g of it. What is the percentage yield?

options.rationale: 60 / 54 x 100. The fraction is the wrong way up, which is why the answer exceeds 100 %.
6 / 60 x 100, the percentage of the product that was lost rather than the percentage obtained.
54 / 60 with the x 100 step omitted, so a ratio is offered where a percentage was asked for.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide that can be made from 10 g of calcium carbonate?

options.rationale: 10 x 100 / 56. The relative formula masses are combined the wrong way round, predicting more product than there was reactant.
Assumes that because mass is conserved the calcium oxide must weigh the same as the calcium carbonate, ignoring the carbon dioxide that escapes.

options.text: 4 g
options.rationale: 0.1 x 40, using the relative atomic mass of calcium instead of the relative formula mass of calcium oxide.
Correct: 10 / 100 = 0.1 mol of CaCO3, which gives 0.1 mol of CaO, so the mass is 0.1 x 56 = 5.6 g.

mcqs.stem: Iron is extracted in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr: Fe2O3 = 160, Fe = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron that can be made from 20 g of iron(III) oxide?

options.rationale: 20 x 160 / 112. The relative formula masses are inverted, so more iron is predicted than there was oxide to start with.
Correct: 20 / 160 = 0.125 mol of Fe2O3, and the 2 in 2Fe gives 0.25 mol of Fe, so the mass is 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.
The value 2 x 56 read straight off the equation and reported as a mass in grams, with no scaling for the moles present.

options.text: 7 g
options.rationale: 0.125 x 56. The balancing number 2 in front of Fe has been ignored, so the answer is half the true value.

mcqs.stem: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?

options.text: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful product.
options.rationale: Correct: atom economy, or atom utilisation, is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products.

options.text: The amount of the predicted product that is collected in practice.
options.rationale: This is percentage yield. The two percentages are taught together and are constantly swapped for one another.

options.text: The amount of reactant that has reacted once equilibrium has been set up.
options.rationale: Describes the position of a reversible reaction, not how the atoms are shared out between the products.

options.text: The amount of the energy given out that is transferred usefully.
options.rationale: Borrows the wording of energy efficiency, which uses a similar sentence about useful transfer but a different quantity.

mcqs.stem: A student weighs out the reactants, weighs the product she has made and divides one measured mass by the other to find the atom economy. Why is this wrong?

options.text: The mass lost when the product was separated must be subtracted.
options.rationale: Tries to repair the method with a correction, when the measured masses should not be in the calculation at all.

options.text: The atom economy changes when the reaction is scaled up to industry.
options.rationale: Treats atom economy as a property of the process rather than of the equation; it is the same figure at any scale.

options.text: The percentage atom economy is calculated using the balanced equation.
options.rationale: Correct: the specification calculates atom economy from relative formula masses in the balanced equation, so measured masses are never used.

options.text: The actual yield of product is needed as well as the theoretical.
options.rationale: Imports the percentage yield method into an atom economy question, which needs no experimental data whatsoever.

mcqs.stem: In the percentage atom economy calculation, what is the bottom line of the fraction?

options.text: The sum of the relative formula masses of all the products in the equation.
options.rationale: Numerically equal to the reactants, but it is not the specification formula and it hides the point that reactants are what must be bought.

options.text: The sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants in the equation.
options.rationale: Correct: the Mr of the desired product is divided by the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

options.text: The relative formula mass of the one reactant that the product comes from.
options.rationale: The most common error: only the reactant the wanted atoms come from is counted, and the other reactants are ignored.

options.text: The total mass of all the reactants weighed out in the experiment.
options.rationale: Replaces values taken from the equation with laboratory measurements, which belong to percentage yield instead.

mcqs.stem: Hydrogen is made from methane: CH4 + H2O -> 3H2 + CO. Mr: CH4 = 16, H2O = 18, H2 = 2, CO = 28. What is the percentage atom economy for making hydrogen?

options.rationale: 2 / 34 x 100. The balancing number 3 in front of H2 has been left out of the top line.
28 / 34 x 100, the atom economy for carbon monoxide, which is the by-product here and not the desired product.
34 / 6 x 100. The fraction is inverted, and an atom economy above 100 % is impossible.

mcqs.stem: Titanium is extracted by the reaction TiCl4 + 4Na -> Ti + 4NaCl. Mr: TiCl4 = 190, Na = 23, Ti = 48, NaCl = 58.5. What is the percentage atom economy for titanium?

options.rationale: 282 / 48 x 100. The fraction is upside down, which no atom economy can be.
48 / 190 x 100. Only the titanium chloride is counted in the bottom line, so the sodium is treated as if it were free.
Chosen by students who reason that because no atoms are lost, all of the starting material must count as useful.

mcqs.stem: Two routes make the same product. Route 1: atom economy 42 %, percentage yield 95 %, fast, by-product is waste that must be disposed of. Route 2: atom economy 88 %, percentage yield 90 %, slightly slower, by-product is sold as a fertiliser. Which judgement is best supported by the data?

options.text: Route 1, because its higher percentage yield means that less is wasted.
options.rationale: Reads the larger percentage as the whole answer; a 95 % yield of a reaction that wastes most of its atoms still wastes most of the raw material.

options.text: Route 1, because a faster rate always makes the process a cheaper one.
options.rationale: Rate is one factor among several, and the cost of disposing of the waste can easily outweigh the saving from speed.

options.text: Route 2, because a high atom economy always gives a high percentage yield.
options.rationale: Reaches the right route by faulty reasoning: atom economy comes from the equation and does not control the yield.

options.text: Route 2, because much more of the reactant mass ends up as product.
options.rationale: Correct: 88 % atom economy with a 90 % yield and a saleable by-product wastes far less raw material, for the cost of a slightly slower rate.
